chapters.title: Study Repeated Patterns of Misjudgment
chapters.sourcePressure: The source frames judgment as shaped by recurring pressures: fear, reward, status, uncertainty, reciprocity, fairness, conformity, missing information, and the wish to stay consistent after public commitment. Munger's two-track analysis gives the working check.
chapters.coreMove: Treat a persuasive live decision as a pattern candidate before deciding it is a special case.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing the lesson to a list of bias names or a smug habit of labeling other people.

chapters.title: Read Human Nature Through Incentives
chapters.sourcePressure: The source stresses self-interest, reputation, reciprocity, fairness, one-shot encounters, approval, humiliation, authority, imitation, similarity, praise, and status pressure as live forces beneath stated explanations.
chapters.coreMove: Read the stated reason and the payoff structure together before trusting either alone.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning incentive analysis into cynicism where everyone is secretly selfish and every explanation is fake.

chapters.title: Use Probability to Resist Overconfidence
chapters.sourcePressure: The source points to overestimated control, desired-outcome probability, ignored base rates, overweighted case evidence, misleading coincidences, margin of safety, and many-path system failure.
chapters.coreMove: Anchor a forecast in base rates and margin of safety before vivid case evidence inflates confidence.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating probability as math decoration after the decision is already emotionally made.

chapters.title: Think Past the First Consequence
chapters.sourcePressure: The source emphasizes systems, intended and unintended consequences, reactions from other people, delayed effects, paying too much, pushing too fast, and failures that arrive through paths the first move ignored.
chapters.coreMove: Follow a decision through reactions, delays, and displaced costs before accepting the first visible win.
chapters.commonMisread: Calling every choice complicated and using systems language as an excuse not to act.

chapters.title: Use Checklists to Protect Judgment
chapters.sourcePressure: The source treats checklists as practical protection against recurring omission when pressure, routine drift, familiarity, or false confidence causes known steps to disappear.
chapters.coreMove: Convert a repeated costly omission into a short situation-bound checklist and keep judgment awake beyond it.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating checklists as bureaucracy, productivity theater, or a replacement for judgment.

chapters.title: Protect Temperament While You Learn
chapters.sourcePressure: The source closes on fear, reward, status, reciprocity, fairness, self-interest, memory distortion, self-serving revision, and the failure to use good tools when social or emotional pressure takes over.
chapters.coreMove: Preserve a gap between emotional pressure and committed action so the better tool remains reachable.
chapters.commonMisread: Making temperament sound like being calm, detached, or naturally stoic.
